title: The butterfly dream
hookLine: Zhuangzi dreams he's a butterfly and wakes unsure which one did the dreaming (Zhuangzi 2)

lines: THE FIRST SECONDS AFTER A DREAM.
HE DREAMED HE WAS A BUTTERFLY.
cards: Some dreams don't let go at once. The eyes are open, but the dream is still there: somewhere else, someone else, maybe, and for a moment the ceiling looks wrong. Then the room settles, and the dreamer is back.

An ancient Chinese book, the Zhuangzi, tells of a waking like that, in its author's own name. It's only a few lines long, and readers have been turning it over ever since. Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly.

teach.b: It's in chapter two of the book that carries his name.

Once, Zhuangzi dreamed he was a butterfly, fluttering here and there, completely happy, doing as it pleased. The butterfly had no idea it was Zhuangzi. Then suddenly he woke up, and there he was, solidly himself.
And now he didn't know: was he Zhuangzi, who had dreamed he was a butterfly? Or a butterfly, now dreaming it was Zhuangzi?
Then one more line, quietly: between Zhuangzi and a butterfly there must be some difference. This, he says, is called the transformation of things. Who was Zhuangzi?

Tradition remembers him as an ancient Chinese thinker, and Taoists read his book side by side with the Tao Te Ching. It's full of jokes, a talking tree, a talking skull, and questions he never quite answers.
This is one of them. It's easy to hear the dream as a party trick: maybe life is a dream! But he doesn't say that.
He says there must be a difference, and calls it a transformation. Scholars have read it in more than one way.
Some hear doubt: how sure can anyone be of what they know? Others hear change: everyone is always becoming something, and the line between one thing and another is softer than it looks.
Either way, the butterfly was completely happy being a butterfly. And Zhuangzi, awake, holds his own self a little more loosely. Not less real.

how: The butterfly dream is read in Taoist tradition as a teaching about change and the softness of the line between self and world, and it is also taught in philosophy classrooms as a puzzle about knowing.

o: a Taoist word for flying free of the body
the transformation of things, always changing
the idea that all of life is only a dream

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: had no idea it was Zhuangzi

s: Zhuangzi concludes that life is only a dream
he says there must be some difference, and calls it the transformation of things.
Taoists read the Zhuangzi side by side with the Tao Te Ching
his book is full of jokes, a talking tree, a talking skull, and open questions.

games.q: you're Zhuangzi. you've just woken from dreaming you were a butterfly. what do you conclude?
o: I can't be sure which was dreaming, and there must be a difference.
games.why: he can't tell who dreamed whom, yet says there must be a difference: this is called the transformation of things.

practice: Remember this morning: the first thing you noticed when you woke, a dream still clinging, the moment before you knew what day it was. Rest in that remembered half-second, before you became busy being you, and notice who's there.
Tomorrow, when your eyes open, before the phone, that moment comes round again.

wordCard.voice: Wùhuà, the transformation of things: Zhuangzi dreams he's a butterfly, wakes, and can't say for sure which one was dreaming.

orig.note: Chinese, wùhuà: the transformation of things, the words that close the butterfly passage.

carryVoice: Your line: who is dreaming. The butterfly was happy not knowing. Fifty days now.
